A sequel is a work — such as a book, film, TV show, or video game — that continues the story of an earlier work. It picks up where the previous one left off and follows the same world, characters, or events forward in time.

Think of it like this: if the original work is a chapter, the sequel is the next chapter. The story is not over; it keeps going.

For something to be a sequel, two things must be true:

  1. It comes after the original work (in terms of story time — events in a sequel happen later than events in the original).
  2. It is connected to the original — same characters, same world, or a direct continuation of the same plot.

A completely separate, unrelated story is not a sequel, even if it is made by the same author or director.

• The Dark Knight (2008) is a sequel to Batman Begins (2005). The story of Bruce Wayne continues from where it stopped.
  • Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets is a sequel to Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone. Harry returns to Hogwarts, and the story moves forward.
  • Toy Story 2 is a sequel to Toy Story. Woody and Buzz are back, and new events unfold.

In each case, you can watch or read the sequel and witness what happens next.
An Important Nuance: Story Time vs. Release Time

The word sequel refers to the story's timeline, not necessarily when the work was published or released.

However, in almost all practical cases, a sequel is also released later than the original. You write the first book, then write the sequel. The sequel is published second because it comes second in the story.

This matters because it helps distinguish a sequel from a prequel (explained below).

Understanding what a sequel is not will sharpen your understanding greatly.

Not a remake. A remake retells the same story again, often with new actors or a new style. A sequel tells a new story that happens after the original.

Not a spin-off. A spin-off takes a character or element from the original and builds a separate, branching story around them — one that does not directly continue the main plot. For example, a TV show focused on a side character from a movie is a spin-off, not a sequel. A sequel stays close to the main storyline and moves it forward.

Not a prequel. A prequel is the opposite of a sequel. It tells the story of what happened before the original. So if a sequel answers "what happened next?", a prequel answers "what happened before all this?" Many people confuse these two, so keep this distinction sharp in your mind.
The Sequel's Relationship with the Original

A sequel depends on the original. This is one of its defining qualities. If you watch a sequel without having seen the original, you will likely feel lost — you won't know the characters, their history, or why certain things matter. The sequel assumes you already know the earlier story.

This is different from a standalone work, which is designed to be fully understood on its own with no prior knowledge required.
Can There Be More Than One Sequel?

Yes, absolutely. A story can have multiple sequels, one after another, each continuing forward:

  • Original → Sequel → Sequel to the Sequel → ...

When there are exactly three connected works, the whole set is called a trilogy. When there are many, the whole collection is often called a series or franchise.

Each individual follow-up in the chain is still called a sequel (though sometimes the second sequel is informally called a "threequel," but this is playful slang, not a formal term).
The Word in Broader, Non-Entertainment Contexts

While sequel is most commonly used in books, films, and games, it can also appear in more general or formal writing to mean any event or situation that follows and grows out of a previous one.

For example: "The economic collapse was the sequel to years of poor financial decisions."

Here, it means the collapse was the direct result or continuation of what came before — it grew out of it, just as a movie sequel grows out of its original film. This usage is less common in everyday speech but worth knowing.

A sequel is a follow-up work that continues the story of an earlier work by showing what happens next to the same characters or within the same world — and it assumes you are already familiar with the original.
